overall:
The entire interview process spanned two days, and honestly, both days were a mix of excitement, anxiety, and exhaustion. We would report to the placement cell around 9 AM and often stay there until 8-9 PM, waiting for our turns and the results of each round.
The actual interviews, however, were surprisingly comfortable. The interviewers were very chill and welcoming. They didn't just focus on what was written on my resume; they took the time to interact with me and understand who I was beyond the papers.
The process itself was quite smooth, but the waiting between rounds - constantly wondering whether I'd make it to the next one - was what made the experience so memorable.
It was my first-ever technical interview and my first in-person interview at CILP, and getting selected on my very first attempt made the whole experience feel almost unreal - honestly, like a movie.
The two days were tiring and definitely anxious, but in the end, the result made every bit of it worth it.

fields.label: Format & Duration
fields.value:
- Online and proctored (webcam + mic on, full-screen lock, tab-switch detection), taken on a HackerRank-style platform through the placement portal.
- Single sitting of roughly 90 minutes, with sectional timers. Once a section was submitted there was no going back to it.
- Two sections only: Coding (2 DSA problems) and Technical MCQs (core CS fundamentals). There was no aptitude, verbal, or psychometric section for this profile.
- Any language allowed for the coding section (C / C++ / Java / Python). I wrote both solutions in C++.
- No negative marking on the MCQs. Coding was scored per test case passed, so partial credit was possible.

- OA was conducted for the full eligible shortlist; results were released by CILP within about 3-4 days.
- Interviews were scheduled roughly one week after the OA, with both PI rounds held on the same day, back to back.
What decided the shortlist: full test-case pass on both coding problems plus high MCQ accuracy. Total submission time acted as the tie-breaker, so finishing early genuinely mattered - clearing all test cases in the quickest span is what put me through.
fields.label: Timeline & Shortlist

fields.value:
- Technical / Coding - 2 DSA problems, Easy to Medium (LeetCode style).
- Technical MCQs on Core CS fundamentals, spread across: Object-Oriented Programming (OOPS), DBMS and SQL, Operating Systems, Computer Networks, DSA theory and time/space complexity analysis, C++ / Java output-prediction and short debugging snippets.
- Not included for this role: Quantitative Aptitude, Logical Reasoning, Verbal Ability, Psychometric or Domain-specific Case sections. Other BlackRock profiles (non-tech / analyst tracks) are reported to have an aptitude section - the Aladdin Data Engineering OA was purely technical.
fields.label: Types of Questions Asked
Questions Asked - Coding
fields.value:
Note: exact problem statements cannot be reproduced verbatim; they are recorded below as closely as recalled, along with the approach that was used.
- Q1 - Arrays + hashing / prefix sums (Easy-Medium). Given an integer array, identify sub-arrays satisfying a given sum condition.
- How I solved it: started from the obvious O(n^2) double loop, identified the repeated summation as the bottleneck, then converted it to a single pass using a running prefix sum stored in a hash map - O(n) time, O(n) space.
- Edge cases that mattered: negative numbers, zero-sum prefixes, duplicate prefix values (store frequency, not just the index), and a 64-bit accumulator to avoid overflow on max constraints.
- Q2 - String / stack-based traversal (Medium). A single pass over a sequence where each element's validity depends on the most recent unmatched element before it.
- How I solved it: monotonic stack, push on open, pop and validate on close, check for a non-empty stack at the end - O(n) time, O(n) space.
- Also discussed (mentally) the O(1)-space counter sweep and why a plain counter breaks the moment more than one token type exists.
- General approach: wrote the brute force first, stated the bottleneck, then optimized. Ran custom edge cases (empty input, single element, all-equal values, maximum constraints) before submitting - this is what produced a full test-case pass on both.

fields.label: Questions Asked - Core CS MCQs
fields.value:
Representative questions by topic:
OOPS: Compile-time vs run-time polymorphism, and which of the two virtual functions implement. What a vtable is, when it is created, and why a base class destructor should be declared virtual. Abstract class vs interface; can an abstract class have a constructor? Shallow copy vs deep copy - predict the output of a snippet where the copy constructor is omitted. Visibility resulting from public/protected/private inheritance.
DBMS and SQL: Predict the output of a query using GROUP BY with HAVING; where WHERE applies vs where HAVING applies. Given a set of functional dependencies, identify which normal form the relation violates (2NF/3NF/BCNF). ACID properties - which property a described failure scenario breaks. Match isolation levels to the anomalies they permit (dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read). Clustered vs non-clustered index; why B+ trees are preferred over B trees for database indexes. Number of rows returned by INNER JOIN vs LEFT JOIN on two small sample tables.
Operating Systems: The four necessary conditions for deadlock, and which condition a given scheme eliminates. Process vs thread - what is shared and what is private between threads of the same process. Paging vs segmentation; a numerical on effective memory access time given a TLB hit ratio. Output of a producer-consumer snippet using semaphores. Average waiting time under FCFS/SJF/Round Robin (numerical).
Computer Networks: TCP vs UDP, and which one a described application should use. The three-way handshake sequence and what happens when a packet is lost. Mapping a given protocol to the correct OSI/TCP-IP layer. HTTP status code classes - what 4xx signals vs what 5xx signals.
DSA theory and complexity: Complexity of standard operations (heap insert/extract-min, BST search worst case, hashing with chaining). Which traversal combination uniquely reconstructs a binary tree; in-order output of a given BST. Space complexity of a recursive vs an iterative implementation of the same routine.
Output/debugging snippets: Pointer arithmetic and array-to-pointer decay in C++. Integer overflow and implicit type conversion output. An off-by-one loop bound producing a wrong result - identify the corrected line.

- Cleared the MCQ section first and at speed, attempting every question since there was no negative marking, then spent the remaining time on the two coding problems.
- Did not chase elegance in the coding section - got a correct accepted solution first, then optimized only where the constraints demanded it.

fields.value:
- Duration: approximately 50-60 minutes.
- Tone: formal but conversational and open-ended. Not stress-based at all - I was given time to think and was encouraged to reason out loud.
- Format: no shared code editor and no live coding. Everything was verbal, with architecture explained on paper/whiteboard.
- Flow: short self-introduction (~3 min) -> deep dive into my Google internship (~25 min) -> Angular and frontend grilling (~10 min) -> projects (~10 min) -> my questions to the panel.
- The round was almost entirely CV-driven. There was no textbook DSA question after the OA - the OA is the only algorithmic filter in the process.
fields.label: Duration & Format

fields.value:
- Walk me through both pipelines end-to-end - the recursive LLM tournament and the cascaded re-ranking RAG. Why two parallel pipelines instead of one?
- Framed it as a quality vs cost/latency trade-off: the tournament pipeline produces higher-fidelity pairwise judgments but scales poorly with candidate count, while the cascaded RAG gives cheap, high-recall retrieval. Both were built so the two could be benchmarked against each other before committing to one.
- How does the recursive LLM tournament actually work? What is the elimination criterion and what does it cost in LLM calls?
- Candidates are paired, the model picks a winner per pair, winners advance to the next round - roughly n-1 comparisons across log n rounds. Also discussed the non-transitivity of LLM judgments and how seeding and repeated matches reduce ordering noise.
- Why embeddings at all? Why not plain keyword or BM25 search over the changelogs?
- Changelog queries are heavily paraphrastic, so lexical search misses synonymy and reworded release notes. I mentioned hybrid retrieval (BM25 + dense) as the practical production answer rather than dense-only.
- What was your chunking strategy across 20K+ documents? How did you choose chunk size and overlap?
- Structure-aware chunking along changelog sections rather than blind fixed-length splits, with a token budget and overlap to preserve context across boundaries, tuned against a labeled query set.
- Which index did you use, and what is the recall vs latency trade-off?
- Discussed exact search vs approximate nearest neighbor (HNSW-style), the effect of the knobs on recall@k, and why exact search is perfectly acceptable at 20K documents but not at 20M.
- What is re-ranking and why cascade it? Bi-encoder vs cross-encoder.
- A bi-encoder encodes query and document independently so vectors can be precomputed - cheap but less accurate. A cross-encoder scores the pair jointly and is far more accurate but must run per candidate. Hence: cheap retrieval down to top-k, expensive re-rank over k only.
- How did you evaluate retrieval quality?
- Recall@k, MRR and nDCG against a human-labeled query set, with an ablation on each stage of the cascade so the contribution of the re-ranker could be isolated.
- How did you arrive at the "33,500+ manual hours saved" figure?
- Baseline manual review time per document x document volume x automation coverage, cross-checked against the team's own tracked effort data. They pushed hard here (see cross-questioning).
- How would this scale from 20K documents to 20M?
- Shard the index, move embedding generation into a batched offline job, use incremental/delta indexing instead of full rebuilds, and separate the build index from the serving index so a rebuild never blocks queries.
- Changelogs get edited. How do you keep the embeddings fresh?
- Change data capture on the source, an embedding version tied to each document revision, re-embedding only the delta, and a document -> chunk -> vector lineage map so deletions propagate instead of leaving orphan vectors.
- What happens when the LLM or embedding service is rate-limited or down?
- Exponential backoff with jitter, request batching, a cache keyed on content hash, and a dead-letter queue so the run is replayable and idempotent rather than silently lossy.
- How do you prevent hallucination in the generated output?
- Grounding by construction - every answer must cite the retrieved chunk IDs it used, and a low-confidence retrieval short-circuits to "no answer" rather than generating unsupported text.
- Explain the hybrid Drive API authentication with 1P Offline Access.
- Interactive OAuth for user-scoped reads, combined with offline access and refresh tokens so an asynchronous background pipeline can continue acting on the user's behalf after the session ends. Also covered token storage, scope minimization and revocation handling.

- The panel never accepted a first answer. Every design choice was followed by a "why not X?" - why not BM25, why not one pipeline, why not exact search, why not REST. Having the discarded alternative ready mattered as much as having the chosen one.
- Every number on the resume was audited. I was asked to derive the 33,500+ hours figure and to justify the 20K+ document scale and the embedding model choice. Bring the arithmetic, not just the claim.
- A one-line mention is fair game. The entire Angular block came out of half a sentence in a bullet point.
- The questioning was designed to separate ownership from proximity - almost everything was about decisions and trade-offs, and very little about syntax except within the Angular block.
- What they appeared to be assessing: architectural clarity, the ability to explain a complex pipeline to someone with zero context, comfort with saying "I do not know, but here is how I would find out", and honesty about the limits of what I built versus what the team built.
- Follow-ups were threaded rather than scripted - each of my answers generated the next question, so a vague answer created its own trouble two questions later.
fields.label: Cross-Questioning & Areas of Focus
Number of People on Panel
fields.value: 2 - a senior engineer and a hiring manager. The senior engineer drove the technical half; the manager led the behavioral half.

fields.label: Duration & Format
fields.value:
- Duration: approximately 1 hour 30 minutes - the longest round of the entire process.
- Structure: two clear halves - roughly 50-60 minutes of a line-by-line technical audit of the CV, followed by 30-40 minutes of HR / behavioral and "technical-HR" questions.
- Tone: formal, dense, and relentless in depth, but not hostile and not a stress interview. They interrupted frequently, but to go deeper rather than to unsettle.
- No live coding here either. Architecture was drawn and explained; SQL and database questions were answered verbally.

fields.label: Technical Questions - Internships Revisited
fields.value:
A. Google internship, revisited at greater depth:
- Draw the full pipeline - source -> ingestion -> chunking -> embedding -> index -> retrieval -> re-ranking -> generation -> serving. Now mark every point at which it can fail.
- Which stage is the bottleneck, and how did you measure that rather than assume it?
- What is your rollback plan if a bad index build ships to production?
- How would you monitor a pipeline like this in production - what are the metrics, and what should page you at 3 AM? (data freshness, ingest volume vs expected, error and retry rates, p95 retrieval latency, and recall drift against a golden query set)
B. Samsung PRISM - Short Text Topic Modeling (a heavy block):
- What is short-text topic modeling, and why does classical LDA break down on text under 50 tokens? - document-level word co-occurrence becomes too sparse for the topic-word distributions to be estimated reliably.
- Explain GSDMM. What is the movie-group process, and what assumption does it make? - a Dirichlet Multinomial Mixture that assumes one topic per short document, with clustering driven by a balance of completeness and homogeneity.
- GSDMM vs BTM - what does BTM model instead? - biterms, i.e., unordered word pairs aggregated at the corpus level, which sidesteps document-level sparsity entirely.
- How do you choose K, and what happens if K is set too high in GSDMM? - GSDMM collapses empty clusters on its own, so over-specifying K is comparatively safe; under-specifying is not.
- Which coherence metric did you use, what is the 18% improvement measured against, and on which dataset?
- Why C++ rather than pure Python for the pipeline? - deterministic memory behavior and control over allocation on a constrained device, plus the eventual need to sit behind a mobile runtime.
- How did you achieve a 35% memory reduction? - quantization (post-training vs quantization-aware training, int8 vs fp16), pruning, and operator fusion. Followed immediately by: what did that cost you in accuracy, and how did you verify it?
- How does a TFLite delegate use the mobile NPU, and what happens to unsupported operators? - they fall back to CPU, and enough fallbacks will erase the latency win entirely, so the op set has to be checked before claiming a speed-up.
- How did you benchmark real-time inference - which device, what batch size, how many warm-up runs, and did you account for thermal throttling?
C. Projects - impact first, internals second:
- What real problem does each project solve, and who is the user? (they deliberately stayed at this level rather than digging into model internals)
- If this went to production tomorrow, what breaks first?
- Which of these numbers are measured and which are estimated?

fields.label: Technical Questions - Data Engineering & System Design
fields.value:
- Design a pipeline that ingests reference and market data from several vendors daily and lands it in a warehouse for downstream analytics.
- My answer: source -> immutable raw landing zone -> schema and quality validation with a quarantine path -> transformation -> curated warehouse tables -> serving layer, all orchestrated as a DAG with retries and alerting.
- How do you handle late-arriving and out-of-order data? - event-time partitioning with watermarks and defined reprocessing windows, rather than overwriting a partition and losing history.
- How do you handle schema drift from a vendor? - a schema contract/registry, additive-only evolution by default, and quarantine plus alert on a breaking change. Never silently drop an unrecognized field.
- What makes a pipeline idempotent, and why does that matter more than chasing exactly-once semantics? - deterministic partition keys plus an upsert/merge on a natural key, so a replay converges to the same state instead of duplicating rows.
- Batch vs streaming - when would you choose Kafka and stream processing over a nightly batch job? - it is driven by the decision latency the consumer needs, not by data volume.
- SQL: deduplicate a table keeping only the latest record per key. - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY updated_at DESC) inside a CTE, filtered to rn = 1.
- SQL: running total, and rank within a group. - SUM(...) OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...), plus the difference between RANK, DENSE_RANK, and ROW_NUMBER on ties.
- Star schema vs snowflake schema; OLTP vs OLAP workloads; when denormalization is the correct call.
- How would you debug a slow query? - read the EXPLAIN plan first, check index usage and selectivity, look for partition pruning, and avoid wrapping indexed columns in functions.
- What data quality checks would you place on a financial dataset? - row-count and freshness thresholds, null and uniqueness constraints, referential integrity, distribution/drift checks, and reconciliation against the source of record.
- Why is data correctness non-negotiable at a firm like BlackRock? - everything downstream feeds client money and risk models, so a silently wrong value is far more dangerous than a failed job. Fail loudly, quarantine, and never half-load a table.
- A few fundamentals cross-checks: SQL vs NoSQL and when to choose each, ACID vs BASE, CAP theorem trade-offs, and normalization forms.

Roughly 30-40 minutes, mostly "technical-HR" - behavioral questions set in an engineering context. Answers were expected as specific incidents, not philosophy; a STAR structure worked well.
- How many people have you worked with on a team, and what was your role within it?
- How do you handle a difference of opinion with a teammate? Give me a real instance and tell me how it ended. (followed up twice for further detail)
- Tell me about the toughest phase you have faced in a development cycle and how you got out of it.
- What was the biggest challenge in your internship, and what did you do differently afterward?
- What is the toughest lesson you have learned so far?
- What factors do you care about most when you productionize something? (my answer, in order: correctness and data integrity first; then observability - logs, metrics, lineage; then failure behavior - retries, idempotency, rollback; then latency and cost; then access control; and finally documentation and handover so the system survives me leaving)
- How do you prioritize when several things are urgent at the same time?
- Tell me about a time you took ownership of something outside your assigned scope.
- How would you explain a technical decision to a non-technical stakeholder?
- Tell me about a time you received critical feedback. What did you do with it?
- Where do you see yourself in three to five years? Are you comfortable working on data infrastructure rather than model building?
- Why BlackRock, and what do you know about our principles?
- Do you have any questions for us?
Most unexpected/most challenging:
- The productionization question. It is completely open-ended and it reveals within thirty seconds whether you have ever actually shipped something that other people depend on.
- The "difference of opinion" question, because it was cross-examined twice - a general answer was not accepted, they wanted the actual conversation.
fields.label: HR & Behavioural Questions

fields.value:
- Every single line of the CV was covered - internships, projects, skills, achievements, and the leadership section. Nothing was skipped. Assume a full audit rather than a sample.
- Two distinct modes: on internships, they went for technical depth and the reasoning behind each decision; on projects, they went for impact and measurement and largely left the internals alone. Prepare for both, because switching between them mid-round is jarring if you have only rehearsed one.
- Behavioral answers were cross-questioned for specifics - "what exactly did you say", "what did the other person do", "what was the outcome". Generic answers were pushed until they became concrete.
- They repeatedly checked whether I separate measured results from estimates. Being candid that a figure was an estimate landed noticeably better than defending every number as hard data.
- What they appeared to be assessing, mapped onto BlackRock's own five principles: emotional ownership (do you still feel responsible after the code merges?), One BlackRock (how you behave inside a team and across functions), passion about performance (do you stop at the first working solution or push past it?), and the fiduciary mindset, which in engineering terms is simply that data correctness is not negotiable.
- The verdict came through the placement cell within about a day.
fields.label: Cross-Questioning & Areas of Focus

overall:
- Full timeline: OA -> roughly one week gap -> both PI rounds on the same day, back to back -> result within about 24 hours through CILP.
- The process is overwhelmingly CV-driven. The OA is the only algorithmic filter; after that, not a single classical DSA question was asked in either interview. What you have actually built is what gets tested.
- Interviewers were friendly, gave real thinking time, and clearly wanted to hear reasoning out loud. Saying "I am not certain, but here is how I would approach it" was received well and never penalized.
- Question sets differed noticeably between candidates precisely because they are drawn from each person's own resume - some were taken deeper into DBMS and OS fundamentals, others further into system design. Do not assume another candidate's experience will transfer directly.
advice:
Preparation advice:
- OA: LeetCode Easy-Medium across arrays, strings, hashing, prefix sums, stacks, sliding window, trees, basic graphs, and introductory DP. Practice for speed, since total time is the tie-breaker.
- Core CS MCQs: revise OOPS, DBMS (normalization, ACID, indexing, isolation levels, joins), OS (deadlock, scheduling, paging, semaphores), and CN (TCP vs UDP, handshake, layers). These are quick marks and they are heavily weighted.
- Highest-leverage prep for this specific profile: SQL window functions, CTEs, joins, dedup patterns, star vs snowflake schemas, ETL vs ELT, idempotency, late-arriving data, schema drift, and data quality checks. This is exactly what separates the Aladdin Data Engineering profile from a generic SDE one, and it is where most candidates are under-prepared.
- Be able to draw every project and internship end to end in five minutes, including where it fails and what you would change today.
- Know every number on your resume and how it was computed. If you cannot derive it under questioning, do not put it on the page.
- Do not list a technology you cannot defend at the syntax level. One line about Angular cost me ten minutes of internals questions - injectables, injection tokens, tree-shaking, change detection.
- Read about Aladdin - what it is, why data sits at the center of it - and about the five BlackRock Principles: fiduciary to clients, One BlackRock, passionate about performance, emotional ownership, and committed to a better future. Map one story from your own experience onto each of them.
- Prepare four or five STAR stories: conflict, failure, ownership beyond scope, a hard deadline, and critical feedback. Every one of them will be cross-questioned for specifics.
- Prepare genuine questions for the panel - both rounds ended on this, and it is an easy place to show you have actually researched the team.
Mistakes to avoid:
- Padding the CV. Everything on it gets audited, including single-line mentions and older projects.
- Answering behavioral questions in the abstract. They want the incident, the dialogue, and the outcome - not your philosophy on teamwork.
- Jumping straight to the optimal solution without stating the brute force and naming the bottleneck. The reasoning is what is being scored, not just the final answer.
- Treating this as an ML role. It is a data engineering role. Frame any ML or research work in terms of pipelines, reliability, data correctness, and measurable impact.
- Under-preparing SQL. It is assumed knowledge here in a way it is not in a general SDE interview.
Strong fundamentals are important, but Juspay's process also heavily tests depth of understanding, problem-solving under uncertainty, patience, and the ability to learn during the interview itself.
overall:
The overall process had 6 rounds, moving from a large applicant pool down to a single offer. The process felt quite different from other companies that mainly test existing knowledge. There was a lot to learn along the way. The interviewers seemed to be testing patience and how candidates handled sudden or unfamiliar questions - whether concepts were understood in depth or only superficially. It was intense and exhausting overall (especially Round 4, which ran nearly the whole day), but the interviewers and mentors were genuinely friendly and helpful throughout.
As with most such processes, the experience depended a fair bit on which interviewer/mentor was assigned and what set of questions they had prepared.

A standard "Tree of Space" style problem: given a complete, balanced N-ary tree, support Q queries of 3 kinds - Lock(v, id), Unlock(v, id), and Upgrade(v, id) - each returning true/false based on success.
Lock(v, id): locks vertex v for user id. A vertex cannot be locked if any ancestor or descendant is already locked by any user, and it cannot already be locked itself.
Unlock(v, id): unlocks v only if it is currently locked by the same id.
Upgrade(v, id): if v itself is unlocked, has at least one locked vertex in its subtree, and every locked vertex in its subtree is locked by the same id, then all those descendant locks are released and v is locked instead. Upgrade fails if v is already locked, has a locked ancestor, or if any locked descendant belongs to a different user.
Had to implement Lock, Unlock, and Upgrade for the given tree and array of queries.

fields.value:
The interview began with my introduction and was followed by his. It was a purely technical interview. I previously interned at Samsung, which was a key highlight of my resume. He asked me about that only because I mentioned the internship in my introduction also. We discussed my project at Samsung and how I got there, my internship experience, things I liked about the company, etc. Then we redesigned my project from scratch (system design), like a verbal discussion only. He asked about architectural decisions in the project, why I used xyz tech and why not abc. Then, there was a discussion around known vulnerabilities in the project and how to fix them. This part took around 30 minutes. I was also asked about core subjects in the middle of the discussion of the project only. So the interviewer evaluated all technical skills based on that only.
Then he gave me a hard DSA question to solve, and I had to explain the approach on pen and paper only (pseudo code). It was a new question, but I was familiar with the pattern and solved it in no time. Below is the most similar question: https://leetcode.com/problems/maximum-frequency-stack/description/
I took the standard approach to give the solution (even though I knew the solution).
1. Don't right away tell the optimal solution; always ask questions like what are the constraints, etc.
2. Then give the brute-force solution. The interviewer will ask to optimize, then give the optimal one. Also, I was asked about time complexity and space complexity.
I was drawing and explaining on a sheet to him (this is a good habit); always draw and explain things when you can. He was quite impressed and told me that it was a great discussion and gave positive feedback.
Tips: Maintain eye contact, look confident, and explain everything clearly without fumbling. Be as real as you can; don't try to make up things on the spot because they can see through it clearly. Also, I referred to the interviewers in all rounds by their name (in corporate, calling by sir/mam is unprofessional). Be comfortable doing so.

fields.label: Duration & Format
fields.value: Approximately 40 minutes, conducted in person.

The technical round depended on the company and the skills mentioned in the resume.

Questions were asked based on the technical skills listed. For example, candidates who mentioned SQL and DSA were asked questions related to those skills.
In my case, I had mentioned AI/ML applications in electronics projects along with Python, so I was asked about machine learning and my projects.
I was asked to explain one of my favorite projects, including its purpose and use case. The interviewer wanted to understand my thinking behind the project, rather than just the models used.
I was also asked about one of my Walmart Hackathon projects.
One guesstimate question was asked: Estimate the number of iPhones in Patiala.
I was also asked puzzles, such as the 2-bulb problem. Company-specific puzzles can be practiced through GeeksforGeeks.
fields.label: Technical & Case Questions
HR & CV Questions
fields.value:
The interview also included resume-based, behavioral, and situational questions.

Questions about my projects and the technologies mentioned in my resume.
Questions about my societies and extracurricular involvement.
Questions about a particular situation and how I handled it.
Questions about challenges in technical group projects and how I resolved them.
A question comparing cash cards and credit cards.
A Tiffany-related question: if Tiffany and Co. decides to open a store in Patiala, what factors will they keep in mind?
Questions about my interest in Machine Learning, as it was mentioned in my projects.

It is important to know your resume thoroughly and not mention skills you cannot confidently discuss. I removed Java from my resume the night before because I could no longer remember it properly.

The interviewer seemed to assess how well I understood my projects, my reasoning, and how I handled unexpected questions.

Project understanding: Be prepared to explain the purpose, use case, approach, and reasoning behind your projects. The interviewer wants to understand your thinking, not just the model or technology used.
Machine Learning: Since I mentioned ML in my projects, the interviewer asked me about it in greater detail.
Situational reasoning: Prepare for questions involving conflicts, challenges, and how you respond to different situations such as your role in societies.
Unexpected questions: Be professional and prepared to handle questions that may be phrased in unexpected or tricky ways.
Guesstimates: Learn a structured approach to solving estimation questions. I prepared for these through YouTube the night before.
Puzzles: Practice company-specific puzzles on GeeksforGeeks.

I learned two frameworks the night before to help answer situational questions:

STAR Method: Situation, Task, Action, Result.
PESTLE Method: Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal, and Environmental factors.

Approximately 45 minutes, conducted in person.

The HR round was conducted by a VP and was the final and most important stage of the interview process. Around half of the 23 candidates who had reached this stage were still in the process.
The HR round mainly focused on resume discussion, behavioral questions, and problem-solving.

The interviewer asked me to summarize my resume and explain my experiences in detail.
I was asked questions about my projects, societies, and overall background.
The interviewer asked me to explain particular situations and how I would handle them.
Questions were also asked to understand my approach to problems and decision-making.
HR & CV QUESTIONS
Tell me about yourself / summarize your resume.
Explain your projects and experiences in detail.
Tell me about your society involvement.
Tell me about a particular situation and how you handled it.
Tell me three reasons why we should not hire you.

The interviewer also asked several questions that seemed contradictory or were framed as traps. It is important to remain polite, professional, and composed while answering.

CROSS-QUESTIONING & FOCUS AREAS
fields.value:
The interviewer seemed to focus on how I think about problems, how I respond to difficult questions, and how well I understand my own experiences.

Resume depth: Be ready to discuss every part of your resume in detail.
Problem-solving: The interviewer wants to understand your thinking and approach to problems.
Contradictory questions: Prepare for questions that may seem conflicting or designed to test your consistency.
Professionalism: Be polite, diplomatic, and maintain your best behavior throughout the interview.
Authenticity: Be professional without pretending to be someone you are not.
Company knowledge: Research the company thoroughly so that you can answer questions about it confidently.

The question, "Tell me three reasons why we should not hire you," was asked as a trap question. Be prepared for similar unexpected behavioral questions.

This was the final HR round, so be sure to prepare both your resume and the company. Stay calm, think before answering, and handle tricky questions professionally.
Know your resume thoroughly and research the company well. Be prepared to explain everything you have mentioned, including projects, skills, achievements, and experiences.
fields.label: Advice

official_role: Product Development – Credit and Fraud Risk (CFR)
advice:
Many companies invite Thapar alumni for interviews if they already have alumni working there. In my case, I had a Thapar alumna as my interviewer in both the technical round and GD.

It is also useful to ask thoughtful questions during the interview to show curiosity about the company, role, and learning opportunities. Always remember to be honest; never lie. It's better to know a little less than to overestimate things.
overall: Always enjoy the process, and try to explain as much as possible in a polite way. Never compare yourself with others; this approach helped me as I was calm and I knew that I was here to learn first as it was my first on-campus interview. I just went in and followed my path.
